fields.reasoning: Builds on @{01M6VYH807FA05BQQ196XC8JPN} (rules in a committed .rhiza/ file, built-in defaults, override targets the ship pick). Shape: the intent has exactly two triggers and the request kinds already fixed in internal/api/request.go (enum feature,bug,milestone), so a table per trigger keyed by kind is the smallest file that covers every case; partial files falling back key by key keep 'built-in defaults reproduce today's behaviour'. Bad names: decision workflows-are-the-rules says Rhiza enforces only references between nodes, and a rule naming a missing workflow is exactly a broken reference, so `rhiza check` (run by make check and CI) catches it before it lands; a silent fallback to ship-change would run the wrong workflow on the owner's work, so runtime failures surface as attention instead. Validating --workflow at queue time reuses resolveWorkflow (internal/api/run.go) and fails fast while the owner is still there. Default kind: change sets from milestone plans and `rhiza change new` are new work, which is what feature means and what the default --kind already is (request.go: 'default feature'). Visibility: run journals already carry the workflow name (run.go Workflow field, run_ls.go), so adding the reason there puts it where the owner's Rex apps and `rhiza run ls` already read, without a new surface.
fields.statement: .rhiza/dispatch.toml has one table per trigger, [request] (a request is queued) and [ready] (a change set is accepted and ready), and each maps a kind (feature, bug, milestone) to a workflow name, e.g. `[ready] bug = "bugfix"`. A key left out falls back to the built-in default (request -> plan, ready -> ship-change); any other table or key is an error. A workflow name no layer resolves is a broken reference: `rhiza check` reports a rule in .rhiza/dispatch.toml whose workflow neither the repo (.rhiza/workflows/) nor the built-in layer resolves (it never reads the personal layer, which differs per machine and is absent in CI, so the same committed .rhiza/ checks the same everywhere), `rhiza request --workflow` refuses it with a usage error when queued, and if a name stops resolving by the time the daemon dispatches, the daemon starts no run and raises it as attention; it never silently falls back to the default. A change set no request opened (from a milestone plan or `rhiza change new`) has kind feature; one a request's plan run opens records that request's kind. Each run records which workflow dispatch picked and why (the request's override, the rule trigger.kind, or the built-in default), shown in `rhiza run ls` and `rhiza run status` and logged by the daemon; `rhiza change show` shows the change set's recorded kind and workflow.

fields.acceptance: A testscript (dispatch-check) shows rhiza check passing with no dispatch file, with a rule naming a repo workflow in .rhiza/workflows/ and with a rule naming a built-in workflow, and failing with a rule naming a missing workflow, with a rule naming a workflow that exists only in the personal layer ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rhiza/workflows set inside the script), and with an unknown table, each failure naming trigger.kind or the table
fields.statement: rhiza check fails on a .rhiza/dispatch.toml that does not parse, or whose rule names a workflow that neither the repo layer (.rhiza/workflows/) nor the built-in layer resolves, naming the file, the trigger.kind and the workflow; it never reads the personal layer ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rhiza/workflows), so the same committed .rhiza/ gives the same result on every machine and in CI
